analysis.one_liner: Lets paid and on-time medical bills count as positive credit history.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on October 1, 2024 and referred to committee, but it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that companies holding medical debt — hospitals, clinics, or debt collectors — are allowed to tell the credit bureaus when a person pays off or settles a medical bill, or sticks to a payment plan [S2]. Credit bureaus and credit score companies would then have to adopt procedures so that this positive payment history actually shows up in credit reports and credit scores [S2]. Millions of Americans carry medical debt, and today it mostly shows up on credit reports only when something goes wrong, like a collection, which drags scores down. The bill would let the record show the other side: people paying their medical bills on time [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are consumers with medical debt who pay it off or keep up a payment plan: their credit reports and scores would reflect that positive behavior, potentially making it easier and cheaper to rent an apartment, buy a car, or qualify for a mortgage [S2]. Hospitals and medical providers who hold patient debt would also gain a new tool to encourage patients to set up and stick to payment plans [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Allows companies that own medical debt to report to credit bureaus when a consumer has paid or settled a medical bill that is within one year of the credit report, and when a consumer is meeting the terms of a payment plan [S2].

Requires credit bureaus and credit score providers to set up reasonable procedures so that this positive medical payment information is included in credit reports and used in calculating credit scores [S2].

analysis.who_pays: No group bears a significant direct cost. Credit bureaus and credit score companies would take on new procedures to incorporate positive medical payment data. The more serious objection is on the design side: some consumer advocates have long argued that medical debt should not shape credit scores at all, since a medical bill often reflects a health emergency rather than financial responsibility, and this bill keeps medical debt inside the credit system rather than removing it [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: No one directly; bureaus take on new procedures

drawbacks.text: The reporting is optional, not mandatory: a furnisher of medical debt information "may" report positive history, and the furnisher — which may be a debt collector — is the one who decides whether the consumer is meeting the obligations of a payment plan, giving the debt holder discretion over the consumer's credit record [S2].

The bill keeps medical debt inside the credit reporting system and directs bureaus to build it into scores; consumer advocates have argued that medical debt should not factor into credit scores at all, because it often reflects a health crisis rather than how someone manages money [S2].
The bill would do nothing for people whose medical debt has already damaged their credit or who cannot pay at all; it only rewards those able to pay or keep up a plan [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real but modest: people who work down a medical bill would get credit for it, which can matter for a mortgage or a car loan. The costs are small, and the main weakness is design — reporting is voluntary and controlled by the debt holder, and it leaves untouched the larger problem that medical debt appears on credit reports in the first place. On balance it is a small, consumer-friendly improvement that was never seriously considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the session ended.

narrative.text: Representative Don Bacon, a Republican, introduced the bill on October 1, 2024, joined by one Democratic cosponsor, Representative Marie Perez [S1][S2][S3].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the 118th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much, because the bill never moved. The credit reporting status quo continued unchanged: medical debt still shows up on reports largely as a negative, and bureaus, score providers, and medical debt holders face no new requirements. Consumers with medical debt got no new way to rebuild their scores.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no one gained much

for.name: Rep. Marie Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 1, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, did not bring the bill to a markup or send it to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor — just two House members in total — and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies and credit score providers
industries.note: Bureaus like Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion would gain more data flowing into their reports and scores and would have to build medical payment history into their scoring models. That helps consumers who pay, but it also deepens the bureaus' role as the gatekeepers whose files decide who can rent, borrow, and buy — a role consumer advocates have questioned for medical debt specifically [S2].

industries.industry: Medical debt collectors and debt buyers
industries.note: Debt holders would get a new way to furnish information: they could report a consumer's good performance on a payment plan, and they would be the ones judging whether the consumer is complying. That can raise consumers' scores, but it also gives collectors a fresh lever to push payment plans [S2].

Providers holding patient debt could report paid and settled bills and on-plan performance, giving patients an added credit-based reason to pay or set up a plan. That benefit runs in the same direction for both sides [S2].
